question_text: A 50-year-old man presents to an ophthalmologist with progressive decrease in his visual acuity over the last 6 months. He also mentions that he has become excessively sensitive to light over the same duration. Past medical history is significant for schizophrenia diagnosed in early adulthood which has been managed with an antipsychotic medication for the past 20 years. The ophthalmologist performs a slit lamp examination and notes discrete brown deposits on the corneal epithelium in both eyes. Which of the following antipsychotic drugs has this patient most likely been taking?

                    ### Question

Past medical history is significant for schizophrenia diagnosed in early adulthood which has been managed with an antipsychotic medication for the past 20 years. The ophthalmologist performs a slit lamp examination and notes discrete brown deposits on the corneal epithelium in both eyes. Which of the following antipsychotic drugs has this patient most likely been taking?

The patient presents with progressive visual acuity loss and light sensitivity, alongside discrete brown deposits on the corneal epithelium. Chlorpromazine is known to cause corneal deposits, making it a strong candidate. Thioridazine is also associated with corneal deposits, but it is less commonly used today. Haloperidol, while used for schizophrenia, is not typically linked to corneal deposits. Clozapine and Ziprasidone are not associated with such ocular side effects. Therefore, the most likely antipsychotic causing the observed corneal deposits is Chlorpromazine, supported by its known side effects related to corneal deposits.
